analysis.investment_thesis: Karnataka Bank is explicitly excluded from the Magic Formula — financial companies distort both EBIT/EV and ROIC calculations. Even substituting ROE as a proxy for return on capital, 11.1% is far below the 20%+ threshold required for a "good business," making the cheap headline valuation a likely value trap rather than a genuine Magic Formula opportunity.
key_strengths: Cheap valuation: P/B 0.74x and Forward P/E 6.06x suggest market is pricing in distress that may not materialize
Strong profit CAGR of 24.1% over 5Y (2020 INR 432 Cr → 2025 INR 1,273 Cr), even if partially provision-driven
Equity base growing solidly: total equity doubled from INR 5,971 Cr (2020) to INR 12,589 Cr (2025)
key_risks: ROE of only 11.1% — well below the 20%+ ROIC threshold Greenblatt requires; mediocre returns on capital at scale
Free cash flow collapsed: INR 1,743 Cr (2023) → INR 570 Cr (2024) → INR 48 Cr (2025); OCF diverging sharply from reported net profit
Revenue CAGR of only 6.8% for a bank — barely keeping pace with inflation; limited pricing power in a competitive regional market
red_flags: FINANCIAL COMPANY — Magic Formula explicitly excludes banks; EBIT/EV and ROIC are not computable or meaningful here
2023 profit spike (INR 508 Cr → INR 1,180 Cr, +132% YoY) is almost certainly provision reversals, not organic earning power improvement — profits since then are flat/declining (1,307 → 1,273)
2025 OCF of INR 210 Cr vs net profit of INR 1,273 Cr — a 6x gap signals low earnings quality; cash is not converting
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Karnataka Bank fails the Magic Formula on first principles: it is a bank, and Greenblatt explicitly excludes financial companies because leverage is their business model, not a capital structure choice. You cannot compute a meaningful EBIT/EV or ROIC when the "assets" are loan books and deposits — working capital and net fixed assets are irrelevant constructs. Substituting ROE as the closest analog, 11.1% is uninspiring. Greenblatt wants businesses earning 20–25%+ on tangible capital deployed; Karnataka Bank is earning roughly half that and has shown no trend toward improvement.

The valuation looks superficially attractive (P/B 0.74, Forward P/E 6.06), but cheapness without quality is a trap. The 2023 profit spike from INR 508 Cr to INR 1,180 Cr (+132%) almost certainly reflects provision write-backs, not a structural improvement in earning power — profits have since stagnated at ~INR 1,270–1,307 Cr. Most worrying: free cash flow collapsed to just INR 48 Cr in FY25 against reported net profit of INR 1,273 Cr, a 26x divergence that signals aggressive accrual accounting or rising stressed assets consuming capital. For a Magic Formula investor, this is not a business worth owning at any price.
